job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Felix Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a master's in mechanical engineering in Stuttgart, and on weekends I'm in my family's workshop in Reutlingen. Weekdays I have lectures and lab, then I eat dinner with my grandparents, who live downstairs in the student-friendly house they own. On Saturdays I help my father with milling machines and then sing in the church choir on Sunday. My internship last summer was at a gear-box maker, which taught me how much trouble a half-millimetre can cause.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mostly noise and the work is still in the workshop. My father would nod and say we've survived worse. At church or choir I wouldn't bring it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think this is the best scenario for me. Machines still need to be built and repaired, customers still want a part by Thursday, and I'm good with my hands and with drawings. I never use AI tools, and a plateau means I don't have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, take a design job at a machine builder near Reutlingen and keep helping at the workshop on weekends. I'd save about a fifth of my pay for the workshop's new lathe. I'd also keep singing in the choir, which holds my week together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels solid. Like a good bench vice, boring and reliable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest pressure on the workshop right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Energy costs and finding apprentices. We've had two apprentices quit in three years because they wanted office jobs. My father says it's pride that's lacking, and I think it's partly pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about apprentices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer more pay and a clear path to the master craftsman title, and I'd talk at the local school. I'd say plainly that machine work will still be there when other jobs have gone. That's an honest argument, not a sales pitch.

say: I'd say it's **mostly noise** and the real work is still in the workshop.
I'd mention nothing at **church or choir**.
think: A plateau is the best scenario for me because machines still need to be **built and repaired**.
I never use AI tools, and a plateau means I **don't have to**.
do: Finish the master's and take a **design job** near Reutlingen, keeping weekends in the workshop.
Save a fifth of my pay for the workshop's new **lathe**.
feel: I feel **solid**, like a good bench vice, boring and reliable.
S0.quote: Machine work will still be there when other jobs have gone. That's an honest argument, not a sales pitch.
fieldNote: Felix is **secure** and his world is physical, local and family-based.
His worry is the workshop's lack of apprentices, not AI.
His choir and church give structure to his week.

steps.text: Take a design job at a machine builder near Reutlingen
Save a fifth of my pay for the workshop's new lathe
Visit the local school to promote apprenticeships

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't love it but it's coming. I'd tell my father that the drawing and quoting side of the workshop will change, so we should be ready. At church I'd say new tools have always shaken things, and people got through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm more concerned about the design work I'm training for. Drawing, simulation and checking are exactly what the models do well, and a machine builder that buys such tools might hire fewer junior designers. The workshop floor is slower to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my design job plans but also spend more weekends learning the workshop's quoting and ordering, so I could take over the office side. I'd try one AI tool this year, probably for the quotes, because my father keeps losing money on bad estimates. I'd also take the master craftsman course on Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels uncomfortable, like when a customer changes the drawing halfway through a job. You adjust, but you grumble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never use these tools. What makes you try one now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only because the numbers say so. If my father loses two thousand euros on a bad quote, I'd use anything to stop it. I'd treat it like a new lathe: learn it properly, test it hard, trust it little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your father think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He says I'm worrying early. He believes the workshop will outlive me. But he also admits his eyes are tired and he'd like someone else to do the estimates, so he'd let me try.

say: I'd say **I don't love it** but it's coming and tools have always shaken things.
I'd tell my father the **quoting side** of the workshop will change.
think: Drawing, simulation and checking are what the models do well, so **junior design** jobs could shrink.
The **workshop floor** is slower to change than the office.
do: Learn the workshop's **quoting and ordering** so I could take over the office side.
Try one **AI tool** this year for quotes and take the master craftsman course.
feel: I feel **uncomfortable**, like when a customer changes the drawing halfway through a job.
S1.quote: I'd treat it like a new lathe: learn it properly, test it hard, trust it little.
fieldNote: Felix is **uneasy** and only tries a tool because **money** pushes him.
He uses a tool metaphor: learn it, test it hard, trust it little.
His father's tired eyes give him a legitimate role in the workshop.

steps.text: Learn the workshop's quoting and ordering from my father
Try one AI tool for quotes this year and check each result
Take the master craftsman course on Saturdays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is not a plan, it's a crash. I'd say publicly that nobody should force this on families and small firms, and the government should stay out of the way but not look away. I'd tell my father to keep cash in the workshop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm anxious. By 2028 design and engineering desk work goes, and my degree loses its worth. The hands-on robots come around 2031, which gives the workshop a few years, but the customers' businesses may be shaken first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the design plan and go into the workshop with my father, learning the trade from the floor up. I'd save every euro, ask the church's job network for contacts and keep my grandparents' house in the family. I'd also ask my father to take the master craftsman title now, because it won't be easy to get later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a fire alarm in the middle of the night. You don't know if it's real but you get up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I blame people who built this and sold it before asking if anyone was ready. I'm not against progress, but a company should have to look a customer or a worker in the eye. Nobody asked the apprentices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your grandparents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the house and workshop are safe, because we own both and have no debt. My grandfather would say we managed after the war, and he'd be right. I'd hold his hand and not say much.

say: I'd say **nobody should force this** on families and small firms.
I'd tell my father to keep **cash** in the workshop.
think: By 2028 desk work in **design and engineering** goes and my degree loses worth.
Robots for hands-on work come about **2031**, giving the workshop a few years.
do: Drop the design plan and learn the trade at my father's **workshop** floor.
Save every **euro** and ask the church network for contacts.
feel: I feel like a **fire alarm** has gone off at night: unsure it's real but I get up.
S2.quote: A company should have to look a customer or a worker in the eye. Nobody asked the apprentices.
fieldNote: Felix is **anxious** and retreats to the family workshop as a hedge.
His blame is moral: nobody asked workers or apprentices.
His family owns the house and workshop debt-free, which holds the anxiety.

steps.text: Join my father in the workshop full time and learn every machine
Save every euro towards cash reserves for the workshop
Ask the church job network for contacts and customers
Push my father to take the master craftsman title now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a fair amount of time, and I'd say people should use it. I'd tell friends to learn a trade as well as a degree. I'd tell the choir that the old ways of working still teach something, whatever machines do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be uneasy but steady. By 2031 I'd have a master's, a master craftsman title and maybe the workshop in my hands. The thinking side goes, but the physical side stays to 2034, and that gives us a window to be useful and have saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work three years at a machine builder, finish the master craftsman exam and take over the workshop with my father. I'd buy the new lathe and one CNC machine, so we can take on bigger jobs. I'd use an AI tool only for quotes, and I'd supervise it myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a long hike with a storm on the horizon. You pack well and keep walking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the plan for the workshop after 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd shift to repairs, servicing robots and special one-off parts that factories can't get elsewhere. A robot can run a line, but someone must fix the old gearbox that nobody makes any more. That's us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this world that frightens you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Customers disappearing. If the machine builders downstream go under, the workshop loses its work no matter how good we are. I'd want my father's contracts spread across more than three firms.

say: I'd tell friends to learn a **trade** as well as a degree.
I'd tell the choir the old ways of working still **teach something**.
think: By 2031 I'd have a master's, a **craftsman title** and maybe the workshop in my hands.
The physical side stays until 2034, giving a **window** to be useful and have saved.
do: Work three years at a machine builder, then pass the **craftsman exam** and take over the workshop.
Buy the new **lathe** and one CNC machine and use an AI tool only for quotes.
feel: I feel like on a **long hike** with a storm on the horizon: pack well and keep walking.
S3.quote: A robot can run a line, but someone must fix the old gearbox that nobody makes any more. That's us.
fieldNote: Felix's plan is **trade-first**, with the workshop as a long-term refuge.
He anticipates a repair niche for old machines that factories can't replace.
His worry shifts from AI to customers disappearing.

steps.text: Work three years at a machine builder, then take over the workshop
Buy a second-hand lathe and a CNC machine for the workshop
Use one AI tool for quotes and check every result myself

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is plenty, and I'd say we should be building apprenticeships and small firms now. I'd tell friends to marry well, work hard and own something. At church I'd say machines are fine, as long as they serve families and not the other way round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel calm. By 2036 I'd be 34, running the workshop and maybe married with a child. The hands-on robots come around 2039, and by then I'd have trained a few apprentices who are good with both a micrometer and a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work a few years at a machine builder, then take the workshop over, and I'd marry my girlfriend Lena, who teaches maths. I'd add robot-service repairs to our list of work, probably with a machine builder as partner. I'd sing in the choir and teach apprentices on Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels peaceful. A long runway with a bright spot at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be different without ten years of warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rush the workshop, take on risk and probably make mistakes. Ten years lets me do things the slow way, which is my way. I'd also have Lena's job as a steady income, which she'd say is not very romantic to say aloud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a good ending look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A workshop with four people who can fix anything, a few contracts with robot makers and a Saturday apprentice who turns into a colleague. And a Sunday lunch with the whole family around the table.

say: I'd tell friends to work hard, **own something** and build apprenticeships.
I'd say at church machines are fine as long as they **serve families**.
think: By 2036 I'd be 34, running the **workshop** and maybe married with a child.
I'd have trained apprentices good with both a **micrometer** and a screen.
do: Work a few years at a machine builder, then take over the **workshop**.
Marry my girlfriend **Lena** and teach apprentices on Saturdays.
feel: I feel **peaceful**, a long runway with a bright spot at the end.
S4.quote: Ten years lets me do things the slow way, which is my way.
fieldNote: Felix's ideal future is **personal**: workshop, wife, apprentices and Sunday lunch.
He values slow methods and sees ten years as a way to avoid mistakes.
His partner Lena's teaching job provides stability.

steps.text: Take over the workshop from my father within five years
Add robot-service repairs with a machine builder partner

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the workshop would have a few years but my degree would lose its worth, and there'd be no time to train an apprentice properly. What would help is a steady rule that small firms get time and support to adapt, and a good apprenticeship path. I'd like the family workshop to still exist in 2040.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd add that people think machines are the enemy, but I think it's about who answers to whom. A machine can't go to church, but a boss can. I'd like bosses to remember that.

headlineQuote: A machine can't go to church, but a boss can. I'd like bosses to remember that.
portrait: Felix is 24, doing a **mechanical engineering** master's in Stuttgart and helping in his family's workshop in Reutlingen.
He never uses AI tools and trusts hands-on work, a good **bench vice**, and slow, careful methods.
His traditional outlook values family, church, apprenticeships and **owning something**.
In the two-year world he is anxious and falls back on the workshop.
With five or ten years he plans a repair **niche** for old machines and a family future.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because his degree would lose worth and there would be no time to train apprentices.
whatWouldHelp: **Time and support** for small firms to adapt, plus a good apprenticeship path.
